title: Impact of fentanyl test strips as harm reduction for drug-related mortality

claims.statement: In the 50 US states and the District of Columbia from 2018 to 2022, a state law making fentanyl test strips legal (16 jurisdictions with a dated law, from June 2018 to August 2022), compared with the same states before their law and with states that had no such law at the time, is associated with fewer deaths from drug overdose than the comparison predicted, in one state-level study (Bhai et al., 2025; no funding, no conflicts declared): about 7% fewer per 100,000 residents (6.7%, 95% CI 1.4% to 11.7%, without adjustment; 7.1%, 3.4% to 10.7%, adjusted for age, rurality and income; editors' calculation from the reported coefficients), which at the death rate in state-months with a law is roughly 2.6 to 2.8 fewer deaths per 100,000 residents a year (editors' rough calculation). With adjustment the figures were similar for White (8.0%) and Black residents (8.4%); the abstract's 13.5% for Black residents is the unadjusted estimate (11.9%) converted with its sign reversed. Unintentional overdose deaths, set against overdose deaths by suicide, homicide or undetermined intent, were 5% to 8% lower, with weak support without adjustment and no difference for Black residents with adjustment (−0.2%; 95% CI −5.2% to +5.0%). This is a study of laws in whole state populations, not of people who used strips: it can show that death rates in these states ran below the comparison after their laws, but not that the laws or the strips caused it, nor whether people who tested their drugs were less likely to die. It did not measure whether strips were handed out or used, it counted deaths from any drug rather than opioid or fentanyl deaths, and it did not allow for other state policies or for changes in each state's drug supply at the same time; a 2026 correction says the authors modified some of the legal dates taken from their source and documented this in an online appendix not read here, and six states that the paper's map shows as legal have no date in its table. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Bhai et al. 2025, Table 3 (log death rate; coefficient and SE clustered by state): whole population −0.069 (0.028) without and −0.074 (0.020) with controls; all races −0.075 (0.030) and −0.078 (0.021); White −0.077 (0.032) and −0.083 (0.023); Black −0.127 (0.028) and −0.088 (0.026). As percentages (the paper's 100(e^β − 1); 95% CI editors' calculation): whole population −6.7% (−11.7% to −1.4%) and −7.1% (−10.7% to −3.4%); White −7.4% and −8.0%; Black −11.9% (the abstract's 13.5% is this value with the sign reversed) and −8.4%. Absolute (editors' rough calculation): about 0.22 fewer deaths per 100,000 residents per month against a mean of 3.03 in state-months with a law, roughly 2.6 to 2.8 per 100,000 a year. Table 4, unintentional against other-intent overdose deaths: whole population −0.053 (0.032) and −0.056 (0.027) (−5.2%, −5.4%); White −0.070 (0.037) and −0.082 (0.031); Black −0.058 (0.029) and −0.002 (0.026; −0.2%, 95% CI −5.2% to +5.0%).
